by: Claude Code (opus), titles and abstracts only

question.intervention: Vegetables, legumes, fruit or plant-based diets
question.comparison: Other foods or diets, or folic acid
question.outcome: Folate intake, status or how well it is absorbed

decisions.reason: Estimates inadequate folate intake in Spanish children and teens, but doesn't compare intake of vegetables, fruit or legumes with other foods for folate.

question.comparison: Ready-made vitamin A (retinol) from animal foods or supplements
question.outcome: How much is turned into vitamin A, or vitamin A status

decisions.reason: Compares vitamin levels by diet adherence in phenylketonuria; it does not look at converting plant beta-carotene versus retinol.
Reviews provitamin A foods and vitamin A status, but only in women and young children, and with no clear comparison to preformed retinol.
Covers beta-carotene and retinol supplements and vitamin A status, but uses supplements not foods, only postpartum women, mostly against placebo.

question.intervention: Vegetarian or vegan diets, or plant foods (algae, seaweed, fermented foods) as sources of B12
question.comparison: Diets that include animal foods, or animal foods as sources
question.outcome: B12 content of the foods, or B12 status in people

decisions.reason: Compares routes of B12 supplementation (oral, sublingual, injection), not plant-based versus animal-food diets or food sources.
Compares serum B12 in vegetarian or vegan and omnivore groups, but only in Seventh-day Adventists, a narrower group of people.
Compares B12 levels on plant-based and omnivorous diets, but only in children and adolescents aged 5 to 18, a narrower group.
Case studies of hallucinations in B12 deficiency; it does not compare diets or food sources of B12.
Meta-analysis comparing B12 status biomarkers in adult vegans with omnivores and vegetarians.
Reviews B12 content of seaweeds, mushrooms and fermented foods, but does not compare them with animal food sources.
Includes vegans and vegetarians and B12 status, but the exposure is B12 intake from diet and supplements, with no comparison against diets that include animal foods.
Reviews oral versus intramuscular B12 treatment for deficiency in gastrointestinal disorders, not B12 from plant foods or plant-based diets.
Reviews case reports of optic neuropathy caused by B12 deficiency; it does not compare B12 sources or diets.

question.outcome: Vitamin C intake or blood levels

decisions.reason: Ascorbate-rich fruits are the exposure, but the outcomes are iron absorption and iron status, not vitamin C intake or blood levels.
Discusses plasma vitamin C as a marker of fruit and vegetable intake, but it is a narrative review with no pooled comparison.
Pooled RCTs giving more vs less fruit and vegetables; the groups given more had higher blood vitamin C.
Plant extracts and vitamin C supplements for H. pylori eradication, not fruit and vegetable intake vs vitamin C levels.
Outcome is plasma vitamin C, but the exposure is measured dietary vitamin C intake, not fruit and vegetable eating as such.
Narrower: 100% fruit juice in children only, with vitamin C intake as one of several nutrient outcomes.
Systematically reviewed fruit and vegetable intervention studies; vitamin C was one of the biomarkers that responded most consistently.
Citrus fruit intake vs oesophageal and gastric cancer risk, not vitamin C intake or blood levels.
Fruit, vegetable and vitamin C intake vs breast cancer risk; vitamin C is an exposure here, not an outcome.
Fruit and vegetable markers vs ischaemic heart disease risk; serum vitamin C is used as an exposure marker, not an outcome.
Reviews blood vitamin C as a biomarker of fruit and vegetable intake, but only in children and adolescents, and vitamin C is one of many biomarkers.
Reports vitamin C intake and tissue levels, but compares Eastern and Western European populations rather than people eating more or less fruit and vegetables.

question.outcome: Vitamin D intake or blood levels

decisions.reason: Meta-analysis comparing vegetarian and vegan children with omnivores; reports lower vitamin D intake and lower 25(OH)D levels.
Systematic review of vitamin D intake and status in children on vegetarian or vegan diets compared with meat-eating children.
Systematic review of vitamin D intake and status in adults on vegetarian or vegan diets compared with meat-eaters.
Systematic review comparing nutrient intake, including lower vitamin D intake, in vegetarian and omnivorous children.
Looks at diet and supplements for treating neuropathic pain, not vitamin D in vegetarians compared with omnivores.
Systematic search comparing vitamin D intake and 25(OH)D levels in vegetarian, vegan and omnivorous children.
Looks at diet after diagnosis and colorectal cancer survival, not vitamin D levels by vegetarian or omnivorous diet.
Looks at diets and supplements for disease activity in arthritis, not vitamin D intake or levels by diet type.
Compares serum vitamin D in children drinking plant-based milk with those drinking cow milk; a single food, not a whole vegetarian diet.
Looks at diet and cancer death in the EPIC study, not vitamin D levels in vegetarians compared with meat-eaters.
Looks at dietary treatments for rheumatoid arthritis outcomes, not vitamin D intake or levels by diet type.
Looks at diet and seasonal affective disorder, not vitamin D levels in vegetarians compared with omnivores.
Systematic review of nutrient status in vegetarian children against controls, including low vitamin D status.
RCTs in healthy adults report vitamin D status, but the exposure is partly swapping animal protein for plant protein, not a full vegetarian or vegan diet.

question.intervention: Vitamin K2 (menaquinones) from foods such as cheese, meat and natto, or as supplements
question.comparison: Vitamin K1 from leafy greens, or less vitamin K2
question.outcome: Heart disease, artery calcification, bone density or fractures

decisions.reason: Vitamin K2 supplements, but only in postmenopausal women with osteoporosis, and outcomes are bone turnover markers, not bone density or fractures.
Outcomes are blood sugar and insulin measures in prediabetes and diabetes, not heart disease, artery calcification, bone density or fractures.
Compares habitual natto (vitamin K2) eaters with low or non-eaters and pools bone density results in adults.
Vitamin K supplements with a K2 vs K1 subgroup, but outcomes are heart risk factors like lipids and insulin resistance, not heart disease or calcification.
Outcome is depression, not heart disease, artery calcification, bone density or fractures.
Vitamin K2 supplements on bone density and fractures, but only in postmenopausal women with osteoporosis, a narrower group.
Vitamin K supplements and bone density in middle-aged and older adults, but K2 is not shown separately from K1.
Vitamin K2 supplements on bone density and fractures, but only in postmenopausal women, a narrower group.
Reviews vitamin K intake, levels and supplements on bone density and fractures, but does not separate K2 from K1.
Bone density with a K2 vs K1 subgroup, but vitamin K is always given together with calcium.
Bone density with a K2 subgroup, but vitamin K is always given together with vitamin D.
Pools adult cohort studies of dietary menaquinone (K2) and phylloquinone (K1) intake against coronary heart disease.
Reviews adult studies of vitamin K2 and K1 intake against coronary heart disease and other heart outcomes.
Covers K2 treatment of osteoporosis for bone density and fractures, but it is a short narrative overview limited to osteoporosis patients.
Reviews trials of vitamin K supplements vs placebo for preventing heart disease in adults; the only trial found used K2.
Vitamin K1 and K2 trials on fracture prevention, but only in postmenopausal women with osteoporosis or osteopenia.
Vitamin K2 trials on bone density and fractures, but only in postmenopausal women, a narrower group.
Pools adult trials of menaquinone (K2) and phytonadione (K1) supplements on bone loss and fractures.
Compares vitamin K1 and K2 supplements on calcification and mortality, but only in dialysis patients, including some children, not adults in general.
Looks at vitamin K supplements and insulin sensitivity, not heart disease, artery calcification, bone density or fractures.

question.intervention: Plant omega-3 (ALA from flax, walnuts, rapeseed) or algal oil
question.comparison: Fish or fish oil (EPA and DHA)
question.outcome: Conversion to EPA and DHA, blood levels, or heart disease and death

decisions.reason: Compares ALA with EPA/DHA in a subgroup, but only in people with CVD and for vascular function markers, not conversion, blood levels or heart events.
Looks at omega-3 intake and age-related macular degeneration, not conversion, blood levels or heart disease.
Reviews vegetarian diets high in ALA against fish-eating diets for blood EPA/DHA, and algal oil for raising DHA status.
Reviews feeding studies of flax, walnut and algal oil for conversion to EPA/DHA and blood levels, with fish oil as the reference source.
Looks at omega-3 supplements for preeclampsia in pregnancy, a different outcome.
Looks at omega-3 and omega-6 supplements for dry eye disease, a different outcome.
Looks at omega-3 and fish intake and macular degeneration, not conversion, blood levels or heart disease.
Pools trials separately for plant ALA and fish-based EPA/DHA on death and cardiovascular events.
Pools trials separately for plant ALA and fish-based EPA/DHA on death and cardiovascular events.
Looks at individual omega-3s and prostate cancer risk, a different outcome.
Pools trials separately for plant ALA and fish-based EPA/DHA on death and cardiovascular events.
Looks at omega-3 supplements for ADHD symptoms in children, a different question.
Covers algal DHA and fish oil in pregnancy and infancy for birth and child outcomes, not conversion or heart disease.
Algal oil DHA trials, but the outcome is blood lipids and there is no fish oil comparison.
Looks at ALA and EPA/DHA and type 2 diabetes risk, a different outcome.
Reviews whether dietary ALA changes EPA/DHA status, but has no fish or fish oil comparison.
Looks at omega-3 intake or blood levels and prostate cancer, a different outcome.
Reviews fish and fish oil against ALA for cardiovascular events and death.
Pools blood ALA and EPA-DHA levels against fatal heart disease, but measures blood levels rather than food or oil intake.
A broad review of n-3 fats across health and disease, with no focused ALA or algal oil versus fish oil comparison.
Reports ALA effects on infant blood DHA levels, but only in formula-fed infants, and compares against standard formula rather than fish oil (EPA/DHA).
Looks at omega-3 versus placebo for brain function, with no plant or algal versus fish comparison and no conversion, blood level or heart outcomes.
Looks at omega-3 intake and women's fertility, not plant or algal versus fish omega-3 for conversion, blood levels or heart disease.
Looks at omega-3 supplements for epileptic seizures, with no plant versus fish comparison and no conversion, blood level or heart outcomes.
Analyses ALA and fish EPA/DHA intake separately in cohort studies, but the outcome is prostate cancer, not conversion, blood levels or heart disease.

Compares B12 and folate intake and status between plant-based and meat-eating diets, but only in children and adolescents.
Compares vegan with omnivorous diets for nutritional adequacy and biomarkers, including B12, but only in children.
Compares B12 and folate intake and status between vegetarian/vegan diets and meat-eaters in adults.
Compares vegan with omnivorous diets for micronutrients and B12 levels, but only in pregnant women.
Pools B2, folate and B12 data for vegan versus omnivorous diets, but only in children and adolescents.
Compares folate and B12 intake between vegetarian and omnivorous diets, but only in children.
Exposure is plant-based milk rather than a vegetarian diet, and B vitamin outcomes are not reported.
Covers folate intake and B12 status in vegetarian diets compared with controls, but only in children.
Outcome is hip fracture risk, not B vitamin intake or status.
Compares the nutrients in novel plant-based foods with animal foods, but does not cover whole diets and names no B vitamins.
Outcome is calcium intake, not B vitamins.
Covers micronutrient adequacy of vegetarian diets in infants only, with no B vitamins named.
Outcome is blood pressure, not B vitamin intake or status.
Reports vegan intake of B1, B2, B3, B6, folate and B12, but compares it with WHO recommendations rather than diets with animal foods.
Outcome is zinc intake and status, not B vitamins.
Outcomes are cardiometabolic risk factors, not B vitamin intake or status.
Reports B12 and folate status, but the exposure is partly replacing animal protein with plant protein, not a full vegetarian or vegan diet.
Compares vegan and vegetarian diets with diets including animal foods and reports B12 status, but covers only children aged 6 months to 11 years.
Reviews the nutrient content of vegan versus meat-based dog and cat food, not diets eaten by people.
